articles.title: Michigan school board votes to ban biological males from girls' sports in major policy shift
articles.summary: Monroe Public Schools approved a policy restricting girls' sports to biological females after Briley Lechner filed a Title IX locker room lawsuit.
articles.body: A southern Michigan school district has voted to restrict participation in girls' sports to biological females, approving a new policy in a 4-2 school board vote amid the ongoing national debate over transgender athletes competing in women's and girls' athletics. "The Board of Education approved a new policy with a vote of 4 yes and 2 no with one board member absent," Andrew Shaw, superintendent of Monroe Public Schools, told Fox News Digital in an email Wednesday. "As the superintendent it is my role to implement the policies established by the Board of Education," he added. "The policy that was approved is for Monroe Public Schools only and does not impact any visiting school." EDUCATION DEPARTMENT RESCINDS BIDEN TITLE IX RULE, RESTORES TRUMP-ERA REGULATIONS The policy, titled "Girl's Athletic Participation and Facilities Use," addresses participation in girls' athletics and access to facilities. A copy of the proposed policy obtained by Fox News Digital states that participation in girls' athletics at Monroe Public Schools would be restricted to biological females, with eligibility tied to documentation on a student's birth certificate. The policy reads, "Participation in girl's athletics at Monroe Public Schools shall be restricted to biological females as documented on the birth certificate at the time of birth. Access to and use of girl's athletic facilities (locker rooms) shall follow the same restriction." The decision comes as school districts across the country continue to grapple with questions surrounding transgender student participation in girls' sports and access to sex-separated facilities. The new policy announcement also comes after Briley Lechner, a varsity volleyball player at Monroe High School in Monroe, Michigan, and her father, Sean, filed a federal lawsuit on Oct. 9, announced by the Thomas More Law Center, raising Title IX and constitutional claims against Monroe Public Schools, the Michigan High School Athletic Association and school officials over the alleged incident. COLORADO SCHOOL PARENTS SOUND ALARM AFTER DAUGHTERS WERE CUT FROM VOLLEYBALL TEAM WHILE TRANS ATHLETE PLAYS BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS Briley Lechner said she filed a lawsuit after she unknowingly shared a locker room with a transgender athlete. "What's very scary is that the day that this happened, I had no clue that there was a boy on the other team," Lechner told Fox News Digital in an interview on Oct. 15. The lawsuit from the Thomas More Law Center "alleges that school officials knowingly concealed from the Monroe High School girls' volleyball team and their parents that the September 9, 2025, match with Ann Arbor's Skyline High School would involve a biological male (transgender female)," according to the legal group. In a statement, Briley Lechner told Fox News Digital, "Our family loves and respect everyone, regardless of our differences. This has always been about my privacy, my safety, and fair play. Nothing more, nothing less." She added, "Every female athlete deserves to have her rights respected and protected. Boys do NOT belong in girls’ locker rooms or girls’ sports. Every girl deserves to feel safe, respected, and protected, both in the locker room and on the court. We should NEVER have to fight for that." WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE Sean Lechner, her father, told Fox News Digital, "The new policy may be watered down, but it's an incremental victory for my daughter and every female athlete. It's shameful it took nearly a year to get here but we still have work to do. Who's to say they can't change it again? Regardless of how some try to twist the narrative, this has ALWAYS been about my daughter's privacy, safety, and fair play. Nothing more, nothing less!" He continued, "Since our lawsuit was announced, my daughter and I have received even more harassing and threatening messages. But at the heart of everything I'm doing is something simple — being a father, being a parent, and loving my daughter enough to stand beside her when she needs me most." He added, "To all parents....put aside your differences, bring faith, common sense, and respect back into our homes. Our children are God's most precious gifts. Love them. Cherish them. Protect them. One day, your daughter may look you in the eyes and ask, 'Why didn't you stand up for me when I needed you?' I never want my daughter to ask me that question. I want her to know her father stood beside her and never backed down. No amount of hate or threats will silence us. I will never stop standing up for my daughter." articles.title: Trump administration sues to block certification of Alaska election
articles.summary: The justice department has filed a lawsuit arguing that the inclusion of two candidates named Dan Sullivan could confuse voters.
articles.body:
The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate race in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.

In a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday, the justice department said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their vote for the wrong candidate.

Polls suggest the race between Sen Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November midterm elections.

The government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Sen Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.

Previous efforts to remove the other Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.

President Donald Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to prevent him from running.

The senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent, and Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both if they are unsure at the ballot box.

In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".

The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.

In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.

"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J. Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.

Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.

In a separate interview with Courthouse News, he said that it is his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".

In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.

Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.

The Senate race in Alaska - which President Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.

The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

articles.title: France braces for another weekend of protests as authorities launch massive security operation
articles.summary: France is bracing for yet another wave of protests this weekend with authorities racing to prevent a repeat of the kind of violence and riots that hit the nation last week.
articles.body: France is bracing for yet another wave of protests this weekend with authorities racing to prevent a repeat of the kind of violence and riots that hit the nation last week. French authorities will be launching a massive security operation with some 70,000 police officers deployed across the country over the weekend, according to the interior ministry. Specialist SWAT units, helicopters, armored vehicles, police dogs and water cannons will all be part of the operation. On top of that, the number of French army soldiers that normally patrol Paris as part of the country’s counter-terrorism measures will be increased to free the police from stationary guard duties. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez issued a stark warning on Friday to anyone looking for trouble, saying the government would be “uncompromising with those who engage in destruction.” Last week’s violence followed weeks of protests over education, dismal job prospects and the cost of living. Initially peaceful and attended mostly by students, the demonstrations quickly turned into the worst wave of deadly, nationwide violence in years. This week, curfews were imposed in some cities to help maintain calm. Bracing for Saturday A large demonstration has been called for Saturday afternoon in Paris and French media are expecting hundreds of thousands of people to attend. The protest is organized by France’s main student union, UNEF, with one of the country’s biggest trade unions, CGT, announcing it would join. Other groups are expected to attend, including farmers, climate activists and the Yellow Vests, the movement that first emerged in 2018 during the protests over fuel costs. While the protest in Paris has been authorized by the authorities, French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday banned all non-trade union protests on Saturday as he seeks to control the civil unrest. But the preparations go well beyond bans and police warnings, especially since last week’s riots sparked criticism of the authorities for not taking the threat seriously enough. The City of Paris announced earlier this week it was clearing public spaces of equipment and materials that could be used to cause damage, including barriers, bins, construction material and other items. Many of the main tourist sites in the French capital, including world-famous museums like the Louvre, the Musée d’Orsay and the Musée de l’Orangerie will be closed on Saturday. Art Basel finished the Paris version of its fair on Friday, two days earlier than scheduled. The Paris National Opera cancelled its performances on Saturday, citing the protests as the reason, and at least two dozen metro stations will also be closed for much of the day, according to Paris municipal authorities. An NFL game between Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints is set to take place at the Stade de France just outside of the capital on Sunday. While the match is scheduled to go ahead, a Steelers fan event in Paris was cancelled by the NFL. During last weekend’s riots, at least two people died and multiple others suffered serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands. French Justice Minister Gérald ​Darmanin said some 2,700 people were held for questioning and 232 have been incarcerated in connection to the riots.

articles.title: European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
articles.summary: An escalation would ‘create nothing but losers’, French foreign minister says as US official warns of possible strike.
articles.body:
Foreign ministers from eight countries are cautioning the United States against further attacks on Iran after meeting in Turkiye to discuss the Strait of Hormuz and other regional developments.

Ministers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany, known as the E3, convened with counterparts from the R4 group of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt on Friday, along with Italy.

Speaking after the meeting in Istanbul, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that none of the countries participating in the meeting approved of another military intervention or attack on Iran.

Such a move would only exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict, he said, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.

A further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters.

“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.

Italy’s Antonio Tajani said the aim was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.

“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he said, noting that “we must promote dialogue” in order to reopen Hormuz.

The warnings came as the US Ambassador to Turkiye, Tom Barrack, said Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran this weekend.

Speaking to X podcast host Mario Nawfal, Barrack said that although Trump is “open and available and accessible to a deal … he’s also been very clear about what he wants”.

Barrack claimed that any potential US military action against Iran would not be aimed at regime change, saying Trump is “interested in rebalancing so that there’s no hostages, no threats, and the world can calm down”.

Reporting from Istanbul, Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu said the eight-nation summit was a “first-of-its-kind” attempt to discuss the parameters of regional conflicts and possible solutions.

Although participating countries “all have different national interests, especially when it comes to the crisis in the Gulf”, the Turkish foreign minister “underlined that what is happening in the Gulf … is affecting the other parts of the world”, Koseoglu added.

The eight ministers discussed Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, escalating fighting in Yemen and prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

The meeting at an Istanbul hotel came as Turkiye seeks to bolster its role in the region, including through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement , the trilateral pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.

Turkiye has said that the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others joining, including Egypt.

Fidan told reporters the pact has “several advantages, particularly because it is informal and flexible and focuses specifically on the issues we face.”

“We are not aware of any other platform that brings together countries with such different geographical and political backgrounds,” he said, noting that Ankara “is well placed to play a constructive role in this process”.

Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the agreement. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi recently said that Egypt would “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and have launched a series of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Mississippi cop who shot 1-year-old boy in Walmart parking lot resigns
articles.summary: The police officer who fatally shot a 1-year-old boy in a Walmart parking lot in Mississippi has resigned from the department, the city’s mayor confirmed
articles.body: The police officer who fatally shot a 1-year-old boy in a Walmart parking lot in Mississippi has resigned from the department, the city’s mayor confirmed on Friday, days after state authorities cleared him of criminal wrongdoing.Sgt Hunter Foster shot and killed Kohen Wiley on June 14 while responding to an incident outside a Walmart store in Senatobia, about 65 km south of Memphis, Tennessee.The Mississippi attorney general’s office concluded earlier this week that Foster’s use of force was justified after a months-long investigation, the Associated Press reported.The state released body-camera footage of the shooting on Thursday, showing the moments leading up to the fatal encounter. According to an investigation report cited by AP, officers were at the store for an unrelated incident when a Walmart employee alerted them that two women were running from the store.The footage shows Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding the child as she and another woman enter a vehicle in the parking lot. Five officers approach the car with their guns drawn. The vehicle reverses, crashes into a parked car and then accelerates forward.Foster steps directly in front of the moving vehicle with his gun drawn. As he jumps out of the way, the car’s wheels appear to turn away from him. He then fires, shattering the front passenger-side window, where Kohen was sitting on his mother’s lap. The vehicle continues moving away.Foster’s attorney, Martin Zummach, has defended the shooting, saying the officer had “no choice” but to fire because the vehicle was moving towards him. In another body-camera recording, Foster tells an officer that he did not see a baby inside the vehicle.However, Kohen’s mother has disputed the claim that the driver moved towards the officers. The women have not been charged in connection with the alleged shoplifting, according to AP.Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the child’s family, has also challenged the officer’s account. He said the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing the claim that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family reached the same conclusion.Kohen’s family and their legal team have called for a federal investigation into the shooting. At a news conference on Thursday, Crump criticised the officers’ actions and described them as excessive.The Mississippi Attorney General’s Office said on Monday that its review found the use of force justified. The Senatobia Police Department said the investigation had found insufficient evidence of criminal conduct to present the case to a grand jury.Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed Foster’s resignation on Friday. articles.title: Mississippi police officer who fatally shot 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned
articles.summary: The Mississippi police officer who fired the shot that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned, a city official told NBC News on Friday.
articles.body: The Mississippi police officer who fired the shot that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned, a city official told NBC News on Friday. Hunter Foster, who worked for the Senatobia Police Department, turned in his badge and gun just a few days after state Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office issued a brief statement saying the fatal shooting was a “justified” use of force. Jada Mayer, who is Senatobia’s human resources clerk, did not say why Foster was leaving the Senatobia Police Department. “The mayor’s office confirmed the resignation,” Mayer said. Foster’s lawyer, Martin Zummach, said in an email to NBC News that Foster “resigned for the good of the city and the police department and to permit the process of healing.” “He is still shocked and sickened that a baby died and emphatically denies knowing a child was in the car or in the front seat and had no idea that those fleeing were suspected of shoplifting,” the lawyer said. While the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has stated that police had been responding to the Walmart to investigate a shoplifting, Zummach wrote Foster was part of a team “investigating an unrelated case involving an adult who had attempted to sexually assault a minor on the store’s property.” “All that Foster and the other law enforcement present were told during that investigation process is that ‘they are running,’” Zummach wrote. The fatal shooting of Kohen on June 14 caused an uproar in this small town some 40 miles south of Memphis, Tennessee, where Black residents have long complained about police harassment. The shooting happened after the officers responding to a report of a shoplifting at a local Walmart arrived and saw “two subjects and a juvenile child fleeing from the store into a vehicle,” according to the MBI. Kohen’s mother, whom her lawyer identified as Vellesiya Wiley, was a passenger. Her friend was driving. Both women are Black, as was Kohen. “Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one,” the MBI said in a June 14 report. “An officer then discharged their weapon and the vehicle fled the scene. The subjects arrived at a local hospital where one juvenile child in the vehicle was pronounced deceased, and another subject had critical injuries.” Kohen’s mother has disputed that account. Her lawyer, Ben Crump, posted a video on social media in June where Wiley said they had gone to Walmart for diapers. She said that her friend was briefly stopped while they were leaving the store and that “I kept walking because it had nothing to do with me.” “By the time me and my baby got in the car, she came,” Wiley said of her friend. They encountered police as they began to back out, Wiley said. “I raised my baby up trying to show them that he was in the car,” she said. In that moment, Wiley said her friend inadvertently hit another car while Wiley’s door was open. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: This is how to use a neti pot the right way, according to ear, nose and throat doctors
articles.summary: Ear, nose and throat doctors explain whether neti pots are safe, how to use and clean one, and who should avoid them. Plus, shop highly-rated neti pots for cold season.
articles.body: With cold and flu season here, you may be looking for ways to ease a stuffy nose without reaching for medication. Neti pots, the small teapot-shaped devices that rinse your nasal passages with a saline solution, are a popular option. They can help flush out mucus and irritants, but if you’ve never used one, pouring water into one nostril and out the other can feel odd or even a little intimidating. To find out whether neti pots are safe for everyone and how to use one correctly, I asked two ear, nose and throat (ENT) doctors to walk me through it. Below, they explain what to know before you start and the steps to follow for a comfortable rinse. I also rounded up highly-rated neti pots to shop if you want to add one to your cold-season routine. Are neti pots safe to use? “A neti pot is a container [typically] shaped like a small teapot, used to flush out the nose and sinuses,” says Dr. Ryan Salvador, an ENT surgeon at Sinus and Snoring Specialists in Austin. If you’re nervous about trying one, the experts say there’s no need to be. “Neti pots are safe and effective when used correctly,” says Dr. Madeleine Herman, an ENT physician and president of the Sinus Center and ENT Specialists of Houston. “They help rinse away thick mucus, allergens and other debris from the nose and can provide relief from congestion associated with colds, allergies and sinus problems.” That said, there’s one rule you should never skip. “The quality of your water is the biggest safety concern,” says Herman. “Never use straight tap water in a neti pot. Use distilled or sterile water, or tap water that has been boiled and then cooled. This is important because organisms that may be harmless when swallowed can cause serious infections if they enter the nose.” The best neti pots in 2026 Before you can use a neti pot, you need one. To put together a list of the best ones, I relied on guidance from experts on what to look for when shopping. Based on what they said, I sourced highly-rated options that have at least a four-star average rating from thousands of reviews. Just note: Neti pots should never be used with water straight from the tap, and you’ll need some sort of saline solution — almost all of the picks below come with saline packets. Developed by a physician, this neti pot has a soft tip that creates a gentle seal against your nostril for a more comfortable rinse. It comes with 30 premixed saline packets, so you don’t have to measure salt yourself. The clear, BPA-free plastic helps you easily see when it’s clean, and it’s top-rack dishwasher safe, which makes cleanup simple. I’ve been using this neti pot for a few years and find it is easy to use, comfortable and small enough that it doesn’t take up much space in my medicine cabinet. If you’d rather not use plastic, this porcelain neti pot is a sturdy, classic option built to last. A lid keeps the solution from spilling (though some shoppers say it leaks a bit), and a small hole on top lets you control the flow as you pour. It includes 50 premixed saline packets, and you can use two at once for a stronger rinse when you’re especially congested. Some shoppers do note that water comes out of the lid if you’re not careful when you tip the pot up to use it. This BPA-free, bottle-style rinse is an easy alternative to a traditional neti pot. Instead of tilting and pouring, you flip it upside down and press a button to start a gentle, steady stream, no squeezing required. It holds 300 milliliters, comes with 30 saline packets and includes a sticker thermometer to help you check that the water isn’t too hot. If you want a more hands-off rinse, try Navage. It’s a battery-powered device that uses gentle suction to pull saline through your nose at the touch of a button. It comes with 30 pre-measured saline pods, which means no measuring or mixing on your own. Just know it only works with Navage’s own pods, so you’ll need to keep buying proprietary refills. This ceramic pot is pretty enough to leave out on your bathroom counter. Each is hand-glazed with lead-free, food-grade glazes and comes in a range of colors. It holds 10 ounces and is dishwasher safe for easy cleaning. It also makes a thoughtful gift. It doesn’t come with saline though, so that’s something you’ll have to purchase separately. These packets make nasal irrigation simple: just mix one packet with 8 ounces of distilled or boiled water. Each box holds 100 premixed packets of sodium chloride and sodium bicarbonate that help you create a saline solution to use in your neti pot. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans buys these for her neti pot after her doctor recommended them. “Depending on how often you rinse, this pack can last a really long time,” she says. “I feel like I haven’t had tore-up in forever.” How to use a neti pot Using a neti pot for the first time can feel awkward, but the process is simple once you know the steps. Herman outlines how to use one safely below. Wash your hands first. Start with clean hands to avoid introducing germs to the device or your nose.Use the right water. Fill the neti pot with distilled, room temperature water, sterile water, or tap water that has been properly boiled and then cooled. Most neti pots on the market have a fill line to help prevent you from over-filling, if yours doesn’t, you should read the directions to determine how much water to add. Mix in the saline. Add the salt packet that comes with your neti pot to the water to create a safe-to-use saline solution. According to experts, if you don’t have ready made saline, you can mix together 1 cup of water with one quarter teaspoon of non-iodized salt (like kosher or canning salt).Get into position. Lean over the sink and tilt your head to the side.Rinse gently. Let the saline solution flow gently into one nostril and out the other. How the solution flows will depend on the device you are using. If your neti pot resembles a tea pot, you’ll need to tip it back to let the water pour out the spout. If you’re using a squeeze bottle, you can gently apply pressure. Or, if you are using an electric model, there should be a button for you to push.Clean up afterward. Wash the device and let it dry completely after each use. Note: If your nose is completely blocked or the process is painful, don’t try to force the water through. Stop and consult with your doctor about other solutions to relieve congestion. How to shop for a neti pot Many neti pots look similar at first glance, but a few details make a big difference in how comfortable and easy one is to use. Design also comes down to personal preference. The features below can help you figure out what works best for you. Material that’s easy to clean. Neti pots mostly come in ceramic and BPA-free plastic. Ceramic lasts longer and holds up to washing, while plastic is lighter and tends to be less expensive. Whatever you choose, make sure you can clean every surface, since you’ll need to wash and dry the pot thoroughly after each use.A comfortable, well-shaped spout. The tip should be smooth and tapered so it fits snugly against your nostril without going in too far. A good seal keeps the saline flowing into your nose rather than dripping down your face, and a gentle, rounded tip is more comfortable for sensitive noses.The right capacity. Most adults do best with a pot that holds about 8 ounces, enough to rinse both nostrils in one fill, according to experts. Many kits come with premixed saline packets, which take the guesswork out of measuring. Just remember to mix them with distilled, sterile or previously boiled and cooled water, never water straight from the tap. Is there anyone who should not use a neti pot? Neti pots aren’t for everyone, and Salvador says a few groups should avoid them or check with a doctor first. People who’ve recently had ear or sinus surgery, or neurosurgical procedures performed through the ears or sinuses should skip them since the rinse can disrupt tissue healing and raise the risk of infection. He also says those with a history of ear infections may develop fluid behind the ears from using a neti pot. Finally, Salvador says people with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of serious infection from improperly prepared water or a neti pot that hasn’t been cleaned well. articles.title: A 19-year-old Australian farmer’s son developed a drone system for moving cattle; his startup raised $1.2 million to expand
articles.summary: A 19-year-old Australian farmer’s son has developed an autonomous drone system to move cattle, with his startup, GrazeMate, raising $1.2 million in
articles.body: A 19-year-old Australian farmer’s son has developed an autonomous drone system to move cattle, with his startup, GrazeMate, raising $1.2 million in pre-seed funding to support its expansion into California. Founded by Sam Rogers, the company uses drones that farmers can operate through a mobile app to guide herds between paddocks without manually piloting the aircraft. According to Forbes Australia, GrazeMate has commitments to muster 1.7 million acres across Queensland and New South Wales. The system also collects information on pasture availability, estimated herd weight and farm infrastructure, including water troughs.How does the Australian farmer’s son’s drone system move cattleRogers described the system as a way for farmers to select a paddock through an app and dispatch a drone to move a herd. He explained, “GrazeMate lets a farmer open an app, select a paddock, and send a drone out to move the herd.” The system is designed to notify the farmer when the cattle have passed through the gate, reducing the need to organise people, motorbikes or helicopters for mustering operations.The technology is designed to operate without farmers having to pilot the drones themselves. Rogers told Forbes Australia that the system responds to the movement of the herd and makes decisions in real time. He said, “Instead of piloting, the farmer simply sets the task and the system executes it, making decisions in real time based on how the herd moves, then reporting back everything it sees.”How does GrazeMate’s drone system collect farm and cattle dataGrazeMate’s system is designed to collect information about farm conditions alongside moving livestock. The drones can report on available pasture, provide estimates of herd weight and assess critical infrastructure, including water troughs. This information is intended to help farmers understand the condition of their land and livestock while carrying out routine management tasks.Rogers said the technology enables farmers to gather information while the drones are mustering cattle. The company’s approach combines livestock movement with data collection, allowing farmers to assess the paddock and the herd as part of the same operation. The system is intended to reduce the need for farmers to manage separate processes for moving cattle and checking farm conditions.How did GrazeMate raise $1.2 million to expand into CaliforniaGrazeMate has secured commitments for a $1.2 million pre-seed funding round led by Y Combinator, with Australia’s NextGen Ventures and Antler also participating. The funding comes as the company prepares to expand beyond its existing operations in Queensland and New South Wales into California.GrazeMate had commitments to muster 1.7 million acres of land across Queensland and New South Wales. The company’s expansion into California marks its move into the United States market. The funding round supports the startup’s development as it seeks to bring its autonomous livestock-mustering technology to additional farming operations.How did the GrazeMate founder develop his engineering and AI skillsRogers formalised GrazeMate as a company in 2025 and moved from working as a farmer to leading the business as its chief executive. He is also a mechatronics engineering student at the University of Sydney. NextGen Ventures discovered Rogers through its network of campus investors in 2025 before participating in the funding round.NextGen Ventures partner Jerry X’Lingson told Forbes Australia that Rogers had taught himself to code in Chinese while working with alternative drones because he could not initially afford the highest-specification models he later went on to build with. X’Lingson also described Rogers’s earlier engineering and artificial intelligence projects, including building a robotic arm at the age of 14 and training an AI model to detect electronic waste.Climbing in the Everest region inspired cattle-mustering technologyRogers’s experience recovering from serious injuries also contributed to his decision to build the company. He suffered a spinal tumour and a broken back, underwent three spinal surgeries and later travelled to Nepal to climb in the Everest region. X’Lingson described the experience by saying, “At 16, [founder Sam Rogers] faced a life-threatening spinal injury. After three spinal surgeries, he climbed Everest.”Rogers told Forbes Australia that observing how Sherpas moved yaks in the Himalayas influenced his thinking about livestock management. He recalled how the herders would climb a hill and ring a bell, allowing the sound to travel through the valley and signal the herd to move. He said, “We’ve been working on how to replicate that kind of natural signalling on a much larger scale ever since.”AI advances and drone technology helping expand cattle musteringRogers attributed GrazeMate’s development to improvements in drone battery life, advances in artificial intelligence and changes in regulations governing autonomous systems. He told Forbes Australia that defence investment had driven improvements in drone batteries over the previous decade, while advances in AI had made edge computing more powerful and affordable.He also identified regulatory changes as a factor in the development of autonomous drone operations. Rogers said these developments were occurring as ranchers faced labour shortages, rising costs and increasing demand. GrazeMate’s system is designed to apply autonomous technology to livestock management, combining drone-based mustering with the collection of information about herds, pasture and farm infrastructure.With its $1.2 million pre-seed funding round and expansion plans for California, GrazeMate is developing its autonomous cattle-mustering system beyond its initial operations in QueenslandYou use AI every day. articles.title: State Department says Trump is 'spot on' with France protests after Macron decries 'stupid' comments
articles.summary: The State Department says Trump is "spot on" about France's protests and mass migration after Emmanuel Macron criticized comments from world leaders.
articles.body: The State Department told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's views on France are "spot on" after French President Emmanuel Macron criticized foreign leaders for making "unacceptable and stupid comments" about the protests rocking the European country. Speaking at a midterms rally on Monday, Trump said that "the migrants have taken over France" and that the country should close its borders following a weekend of anti-government demonstrations that evolved into rioting and looting. He added that France, a "once great nation," is "being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Macron then claimed Wednesday that "there was foreign manipulation of information" following the protests, including AI-generated images that showed scenes that never happened in France, which gave way to "unacceptable and stupid comments from many people including foreign leaders." Macron said he was referring to Trump, "among others," and also mentioned, "We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false," The Associated Press reported. When asked for a reaction to Macron's remarks, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital that Trump "is on point as he is consistently on point." "He has been clear about the dangers of mass migration for years, especially since the beginning of this administration, but certainly long beforehand as well. The president has secured the border on day one when it comes to the United States of America," Pigott said. "But we've also been clear from the State Department's perspective that we are going to oppose international institutions, for example, that seek to impose an agenda upon sovereign nations to encourage mass migration. FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' "Mass migration is inherently destabilizing. It is inherently destabilizing. It is something that we don't believe solves problems, but actually creates problems. And this is something the president has raised time and time again. He's raised it in reaction to these recent protests," Pigott added. "He's also raised it directly to world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly. Two years in a row raising this issue, calling for an end to the destructive policies of illegal amassed migration. Illegal amassed migration that, by the way, only helps criminal cartel groups. That's something we see in our own hemisphere, for example," Pigott continued. "The fact that cartel groups have traveled along these migration pathways. So the president is spot on, he's bringing attention to this issue, he is taking action to address this issue and, from the State Department's perspective, we have also taken concrete action to end the era of mass migration." FRANCE'S RIOT CHAOS FUELS FARAGE'S WARNING THAT MASS IMMIGRATION FAILURES COULD HAUNT ANOTHER COUNTRY NEXT The Louvre and other major museums in Paris will be closed on Saturday as more protests are scheduled in the French capital, according to the AP. Reuters also reported that businesses in central Paris have started boarding up their windows over concerns of violence. French officials said more than 3,000 shops were looted, and some 2,500 people were taken into police custody in connection to last weekend's nationwide protests. "One of things that we really stress to Americans is that when they're traveling abroad, if they could please register for the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). That program lets you tell us which countries you're going to so that we can provide real-time information to Americans in the country that have registered," Pigott told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "Speaking generally, when it comes to Americans that need assistance, we have personnel across the world at the State Department, at embassies and consulates that are working 24/7 to help the American people. If you have an issue when you're abroad, please contact the embassy or consulate," he added. "There are people that are there to help you that can provide information. Everything from a lost passport to responses to a security situation, that is something that is hugely important and a huge factor for the State Department."

articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejects US allegations of election interference ahead of the midterm elections, emphasizing Canada's commitment to independent politics. Tensions between Canada and the US escalate over trade negotiations and tariffs.
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected allegations that Ottawa intends to interfere in the upcoming US midterm elections, criticising Washington’s ambassador for suggesting that Canadian officials were seeking to influence American politics.Speaking to reporters during an official visit to Turkey on Friday, Carney said Canada had no plans to intervene in the November 3 elections and dismissed the accusations as unfounded.“There is no merit to these claims,” he said. “I'm disappointed their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions.”The dispute adds to tensions between the neighbouring countries following the collapse of trade negotiations in August. Canada withdrew from discussions over a potential agreement, citing what it described as unreasonable demands from the US.The US embassy in Canada criticised Ottawa on Wednesday, accusing Canadian officials of brushing aside concerns about election interference while ministers and provincial premiers openly discussed plans to influence American politics.A week earlier, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra had urged Canadians to stay out of US political affairs during a podcast appearance. “Keep your nose out of American politics,” he said.Carney’s comments come as relations remain strained over trade and US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada. Washington has also imposed a series of tariffs on Canadian imports, adding pressure to the economic relationship between the two countries.Asked whether Trump might respond to poor Republican results by imposing additional tariffs on Canada, Carney said he did not believe that was likely.The trade negotiations abandoned in August had included efforts to reduce some of the existing tariffs. Carney said Canada was not under pressure to reach a new agreement and suggested, for the first time, that Ottawa could wait until Trump leaves office to secure a deal.“If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that,” he said.Carney’s visit to Turkey is part of a broader effort to reduce Canada’s economic dependence on the US. The two countries have deep trade ties, but the dispute over tariffs and the future of negotiations has added urgency to Ottawa’s push to diversify its economic relationships.Rejecting the prospect of Canada becoming part of the United States, Carney said his government would continue to pursue an independent course.“It's absolutely clear where I stand, where Canada stands, where Canadians stand. articles.title: We swapped streaming for the $99 Lola CD player — here’s our honest review
articles.summary: We tested the Lola CD Player for two weeks to see how it measures up to streaming services. Here’s who it’s best for and whether it’s worth the price.
articles.body: Listening to music is easier than ever — you have hundreds of thousands of songs at your fingertips, plus, algorithms, custom playlists, pre-saves and more make the process feel automated. However, that doesn’t mean we’re ready to give up on physical media. A 2025 Consumer Reports study found that almost half of Americans (45%) still listen to CDs, with one in five still listening to vinyl records. The Lola CD player is designed to help bring that nostalgic feel back to your music, and myself, along with three other NBC Selected editors, tested it for two weeks. We collectively agree that it’s a fun way to switch up our listening habits (and a very cute accessory to carry around), however, it may not be best for people most concerned with convenience. Keep reading to hear our thoughts and our final verdict on the CD player’s highs and lows. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What to know about the Lola Portable CD Player The Lola CD player is a classic portable player with a few modern updates, including anti-skip protection and a micro SD card slot. It charges via an included USB-C cable, so you can share a charger with your phone if needed. While the player doesn’t have Bluetooth capabilities, it has a 3.5mm headphone jack, and can be paired with a Bluetooth device with a third-party adapter, according to the brand. It also comes with a pair of polka dot, wired headphones, and gets up to 48 hours of playback on a single charge. How we tested it Four NBC Selected editors, myself included, tested courtesy samples for around two weeks, using it as a substitute for streaming music. We listened on commutes, on walks and throughout the day to see how the listening experience measured up. Since a few of us belong to different generations, we all have a range of experiences with physical media, helping to shape each of our unique perspectives on using the CD player. While I’ve owned boomboxes and CD players in the past, two of our editors grew up listening to CDs, which made this testing process especially interesting for them. “I’m in my late 30s, and grew up recording songs off the radio onto cassette tapes and listening to them on my Walkman,” says NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown. “I eventually graduated to CDs, most of which I still have today — and of course I took my CD player everywhere,” she says. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans had a similar experience — “I’m a Xennial, so I had a Discman in high school and remember burning mixtapes in college,” she says. “I praised the day the iPod dropped and changed the way we listened to music”. NBC Selected editorial operations associate (and Gen-Z-er) Jem Alabi, on the other hand, specifically likes buying physical versions of her favorite K-pop albums, but hasn’t had anything to play them on until now. “I have quite a few CD’s that have been collecting dust,” she says. “The CD’s tend to have bonus tracks that you can’t always find on streaming so I was happy to get to hear my favorite groups in this intimate way.” Along with seeing how well the CD player works in comparison to streaming, we also evaluated features like the battery life and the player’s anti-skip protection. What we liked In our experience, the Lola CD player is worth it for anyone looking to invest more in physical media, or who may be searching for a more intimate and intentional music listening experience than streaming can offer. We also like the anti-skip protection and battery life. While those features work well, we felt as though our experiences with the headphones were mixed, and that the CD player, while cute, isn’t very convenient to carry around. An intentional way to connect with music The Lola CD player definitely feels like a throwback to a simpler time — pre-streaming and algorithms, when your listening experience felt a lot more personal and manual. I especially felt this during the time when I’d choose my CDs for the day — I usually chose one to start with inside the player, and then one more to bring along for variety. Choosing the CD every morning felt like I was curating my mood for the day, which added an intentionality to my music listening that isn’t always there with streaming. “Using this CD player felt like stepping into a time machine,” says Brown. “I pulled out my CD case and immediately was transported to all that was happening in my life when I made or bought each one — the people I was spending time with, the city I lived in, the party I pregamed for, the person I was dating.” She also turned it into a communal experience: “I started sending pictures of CDs to my group chat and we went down rabbit holes seeing what certain singers and musicians were up to since we last listened to them.” she says. Evans felt similarly, saying that using the CD player shifted her daily listening habits from single songs to full albums. “I also rediscovered songs that I loved and hadn’t heard in forever because I rarely play full albums all the way out (versus spot-playing songs from different albums),” she says. Alabi, who grew up listening to Afrobeat CDs with her family, also felt that the CD player helped her reconnect with those memories: “My family has a vast Afrobeat CD collection with songs that marked my childhood but can’t be found on streaming, so it was cool to have a way to preserve and revive those memories,” she says. That’s also something I loved about the CD player — it let me finally put so many of my old CDs to use while on-the-go, instead of letting them collect dust on my shelves (and made me look forward to picking up some new ones, too). Surprisingly, no skips (for the most part) Prior to testing, one of Evans’ biggest concerns was whether or not the player would skip, or damage her CDs. Thankfully, the device’s anti-skip protection did its job well, which she calls “a huge plus”. She was also reminded that since the music didn’t rely on a Wi-Fi connection, there were no service outages. “This does not go down in ‘dead zones’ the way streaming does and that was a nice change,” she says. I also didn’t experience any skipping, which I fully expected, since it was such a common part of my experience with CD players when I was younger. “I experienced skipping but only because I was listening to my mixed CDs that I would literally just throw into bags and commute with, without protection (ah, to be young!),” says Brown. Long battery life I used the CD player for a few hours daily, and only had to charge it every few days. As someone who charges their phone not only overnight, but constantly throughout the day, it was nice to have a device that I didn’t have to think about plugging in. I also like that I didn’t feel the need to bring along the charger, like I do with my phone, since I knew the battery wouldn’t run out on me. Brown, who used the player every few days, had a similar experience and says hers still wasn’t close to needing another charge at the time of giving feedback. Potential drawbacks to keep in mind Headphones have mixed sound quality Our experiences with the headphones were varied. Brown, who doesn’t care too deeply about sound quality, says she thought the listening experience was good, and Evans felt similarly. “It was as good as any other device I use today,” says Evans. I, on the other hand, wasn’t a big fan of the sound quality, and felt the headphones had a far-away sound, as if you were listening through a wall. Alabi felt similarly, saying that she thought “the headphones were cute but they felt and sounded kind of cheap, like the ones you get on the airplane.” “I recommend using or buying another pair to enhance the listening experience,” she says. We also all felt that in our experience, the volume, although not overpoweringly loud, was loud enough to be heard outside of the headphones. “People can clearly hear what you’re listening to and it’s loud since the corded earbuds don’t have ANC,” says Evans. Not travel friendly While the Lola CD player itself isn’t bulky, we didn’t exactly find it to be compact or slim either. If you’re carrying a larger or medium-sized bag, it shouldn’t pose any issues — “it’s kind of bulky but it did slide right into my bag with my laptop and planner,” says Evans. However, if you’re looking to carry along a mini bag (as I often do when I’m not at the office), you’ll either have to hold it in your hands, or leave the CD player behind. The other size/portability consideration comes with the CDs. Again, you either have to choose to commit to one, or commit to carrying multiple around with you. Although the player’s CD card insert is designed to bypass that problem, you still have to load the memory cards with songs, which adds another manual step that streaming doesn’t require. Is the Lola portable CD player worth it? The Lola portable CD player is worth it if you’re looking to add a vintage twist to your music listening experience. It may not be ideal if you’re used to the convenience of streaming, but at its current price of $99, it’s best for those who either haven’t owned one before and would like to try, or who are trying to recapture the nostalgia of a bygone era. “This is definitely more for someone who never knew what it was to lug around a book of CDs just to get through an hour-long commute,” says Evans. On the other hand, she also says that “one of the biggest pluses to this is rediscovering songs on full albums that I haven’t heard in so long and kind of forgot about (but love).” Brown agrees that the CD player has a universal appeal. “CD players are for everyone,” she says. “There’s something positive to be taken from the experience of using one, regardless of your age or background.” Alternatives to consider When it comes to retro tech, Urban Outfitters is one of my favorite destinations for browsing — the retailer has a wide range of options that are designed to be nostalgic, but with a modern twist. If you’re looking to recreate the CD experience at home, consider bookshelf players and boomboxes like the affordable Jenson CD590 boombox, or the more versatile Emerson EDL-2901 Multi-Media Boombox. You can also double down on the nostalgia and go for a record player, like the Crosley Eclipse Entertainment Center. If portability is what you’re after, MoMA Design Store’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has a cool transparent design, or you can get an MP3 player like the Globluum MP3 Player from Amazon. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected, covering skin care, lifestyle and more, along with being a longtime music fan and collector of records, CDs, magazines and more. I’ve written about why I love my old Sony bookshelf CD player, along with my Audio-Technica record player, and for this piece, myself and three other NBC Selected staffers tried out the Lola portable CD player, to see how the vintage device would hold up against our modern music habits. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
articles.summary: The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine.
articles.body: The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection. “As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service. The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.” “Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added. Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it. President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied. A second drone pilot, serving in the eastern Kharkiv region, said that Ukraine does not have an alternative that’s as effective as Starlink for flying drones, but it also affects the unit’s movements — and ultimately survival chances out in the field. “When we drive into a position, we have a Starlink Mini mounted on the vehicle, and we always try to get there as fast as possible, because if we drive slowly, the enemy will spot us and a drone will catch up with us,” said the pilot, who also only wanted to be identified by his call sign, Dovbush. “So we try to drive fast, but when we drive fast, the connection drops.” That leaves them with a radio as the only alternative for communication, Dovbush, 31, said, while a lack of reliable connection has impacted reconnaissance drones used to identify targets, he added. “It’s a knife in the back,” Flint, the drone unit commander, said of the apparent withdrawal of U.S. support. He said his unit relies on Starshield to fly attack and reconnaissance drones at anything from Russian troops to command posts to tanks. “Its primary role is maintaining the connection with the drone, so this is a very significant loss for us,” he added. Should Starshield restrictions continue, a large portion of their drones will never even get off the ground, he said, while others will be highly vulnerable, flying at lower speeds. “They could practically be swatted out of the sky with a stick,” he said. “And the scariest part is that all this is happening against the backdrop of offensive operations on many areas of the front line, including ours,” he added. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that restrictions on Starlink were still in place, but that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him it would be fully back in about 48 to 72 hours. Before the latest collapse in relations with Washington, Ukraine’s military had been chipping away at land seized by Russia in the eastern Donetsk region, part of the Donbas heartland that the Kremlin has been struggling to capture. In one major operation, more than 100 square miles of territory and 16 settlements have been reclaimed, Ukrainian officials have said, crediting methods like using bomber drones to fly robot vehicles behind enemy lines. The offensive — dubbed Operation Vivaldi — was made public several weeks before the drastic turn from the United States. Trump has agreed to a diesel deal with Russia, waived sweeping new sanctions and seen his peace envoy laud Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian.” Ukraine accused the U.S. of briefly withholding intelligence warnings about Russian attacks, and has said the Starlink slowdown has affected battlefield missions. The U.S. has vehemently denied freezing Ukraine out, but the slew of dramatic developments have left Ukrainian troops disheartened. NBC News spoke with five soldiers, mostly drone operators, who said they felt betrayed by the U.S., and Trump in particular. Ukrainian officials say that the offensive has disrupted Russia’s assault on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, key Ukrainian strongholds in the Donbas region. “We prevented the enemy from flanking the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration and trapping it in a pincer movement,” said Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, which led the operation. The offensive, in which Biletskyi said some 8.000 Russian troops were killed, saw Ukraine use bomber drones to deliver robot vehicles deep behind enemy lines and convert Soviet-era armored personnel carriers into exploding units to “blow up the enemy’s most heavily fortified positions,” he added. “That was us,” a Ukrainian drone pilot told NBC News as he said his unit was redeploying elsewhere. “Our reconnaissance drone positions moved forward every three weeks,” the soldier, 24, who only wanted to be identified by his call sign Lucky because of the sensitive nature of his service, said in a series of audio messages on WhatsApp. During a meeting with his army chiefs last week, Putin said Russian forces were on the offensive along the entire front line. “The pace of advancement has increased significantly,” he added. But George Barros, a senior Russia analyst with the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War, which has provided daily analysis of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, said they assess that Russia has seized a net of only about 40 square miles across all of Ukraine since the beginning of the year. “That means that the daily average Russian rate of advance is far below 0.4 square miles per day. This is a literal foot-pace advance,” he said. “In the month of September, we observed evidence to assess that the Ukrainians actually liberated and took back more territory than the Russians did.” Putin’s army chief, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, told the Russian leader that the Ukrainian offensive was a series of “PR stunts” that achieved nothing and cost Ukraine 3,500 troops who had been either killed or wounded. But Barros said the offensive allowed Ukraine to push forward with tanks and armored personnel carriers into the drone-dominated battlefield, negate Russian drone defenses and find ways to push its forces forward and make gains. Critically, it stopped the northern encirclement of the stronghold cities in Donetsk, putting a wrench in Putin’s plans to complete the capture of Donbas this year, military experts said. “Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi was unquestionably a major success,” said Rajan Menon, senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies. But the Starshield slowdown is a “severe problem for Ukraine,” Menon said, “and a godsend for Putin.” If the restrictions continue for the medium- to long-term, Russian forces will be able to restore their logistics in the regions close to the front line that they control and that Ukraine has been pummeling with middle-range strikes this year, Barros said. As a result, Russia could regain resources to push forward with greater operational tempo, he added, increasing the likelihood of a breakthrough. But at least two of the soldiers interviewed told NBC News that Starlink was not slowed down universally across the front lines. A drone technician serving in Donetsk, who also asked not to be named due to the sensitive nature of his service, said his unit hasn’t seen any major drops in performance. “Given the recent weather, the speed dips and service seemed normal,” the soldier, 31, said, adding that he was aware that other units were experiencing difficulties. The Pentagon responded to NBC News’ request for comment on the soldiers’ criticisms by referring to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s remarks Wednesday in which he reiterated that the U.S. has not changed its posture toward Ukraine in any way, calling its fight against Russia “a heroic effort.”

articles.title: In 2018, Portia de Rossi surprised Ellen DeGeneres with a gorilla conservation project; by September 2023, its Rwanda campus had welcomed over 40,000 visitors, including more than 7,500 local schoolchildren
articles.summary: When actress Portia de Rossi surprised her wife, television host Ellen DeGeneres, with a 60th birthday gift in 2018, she helped fund a major conservation
articles.body: When actress Portia de Rossi surprised her wife, television host Ellen DeGeneres, with a 60th birthday gift in 2018, she helped fund a major conservation project in Rwanda. The project improved wildlife protection and gave local people more chances to learn about the environment. By September 2023, the Ellen DeGeneres Campus of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund had welcomed more than 40,000 visitors to its site outside Volcanoes National Park. During the same period, the educational centre hosted more than 7,500 Rwandan schoolchildren, giving them access to practical science lessons and conservation training. The project began as a gift inspired by DeGeneres' long-standing admiration for pioneering primatologist Dian Fossey. It later grew into a permanent, 12-acre research centre designed to protect endangered mountain gorillas and support nearby communities.Birthday gift sparks conservation initiativeDuring a 2018 recording of The Ellen DeGeneres Show, de Rossi announced the creation of The Ellen Fund and a partnership with the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund. The project promised to build a permanent home for the Fossey Fund, which had worked from rented buildings in Rwanda for decades after Fossey's death in 1985. In a report about the television appearance, WTVR CBS 6 described how DeGeneres began to cry when she learned about the gift. "I've always been passionate about helping animals," DeGeneres said in a statement released at the time. "Nobody knows this more than my wife, and she knew the exact right gift to give me". Dr. Tara Stoinski, president and chief executive officer of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund, spoke about the importance of the partnership. "It's impossible to overstate what this news means for us," Dr. Stoinski told the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund news outlet during the 2018 announcement.Modern campus opens in RwandaConstruction of the multi-building centre began in 2019. The project focused on sustainable design, planting native trees and plants, and using environmentally friendly building methods. The Ellen DeGeneres Campus officially opened in February 2022, welcoming scientists, tourists and students. The centre includes modern laboratories, a scientific library, classrooms, interactive public exhibits and accommodation for visiting researchers. More than 250,000 native plants were planted across the grounds to help restore natural habitats around the park boundary. According to figures shared by Discovery Channel and reported by The Futon Critic, about half of all visitors to the campus during its first 18 months were Rwandan citizens and local students. This showed the centre's importance as an educational resource for the surrounding region.Documenting the conservation journeyThe five-year journey from de Rossi's original surprise gift to the opening of the centre was recorded in a television special called Saving the Gorillas: Ellen's Next Adventure. Entertainment Tonight reported that the documentary premiered on Discovery Channel and Animal Planet in September 2023 to mark World Gorilla Day. It showed behind-the-scenes footage of the construction work, close encounters with wild mountain gorilla families and interviews with field biologists. The documentary also explained how continued conservation efforts had helped mountain gorilla numbers grow in the wild. Mountain gorillas are among the few wild ape species whose populations have increased.Educational reach and community impactWorking with local communities remains a key part of the campus's mission. The centre offers free conservation programs, computer lab access and science workshops for primary and secondary school students living near gorilla habitats. Beyond school education, the campus also offers research internships for Rwandan university students studying biology and environmental science. The Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund confirmed that the campus would continue to expand its community programs. These efforts aim to build local skills and knowledge while supporting ongoing gorilla monitoring and anti-poaching patrols throughout Volcanoes National Park. For a closer look at how the project developed, viewers can watch the trailer for Saving the Gorillas. It offers a preview of the Discovery documentary, including the construction of the Rwanda campus and conservation work in the field.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: In blue Maine, nobody believes Susan Collins will lose until they see it
articles.summary: Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's senate race, but voters in Bangor say her three decades of familiarity may be impossible to beat.
articles.body: There are two elements of the Senate race in Maine that truly stand out on the ground. One is that this is a small state, at least in terms of population. The other is that Susan Collins has been a senator here for three decades. The upshot is that almost everyone I've met here has met her. Philip, a lifelong Mainer in his 70s from Bangor, told me in an accent straight out of "Murder, She Wrote": "It would be stupid, in my opinion, not to vote for Susan, she's chairman of the appropriations committee, and she's brought a lot of money to the state," adding, "we've got new fire stations in every little town you can think of." The appreciation for Collins among ordinary Mainers represents the daunting uphill battle Democrat Troy Jackson faces in a race where polls give him a slight lead, but the word on the street has him dead in the water. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' Speaking of fire stations, I met Andy and Hank, both firefighters, at Seasons restaurant in Bangor. And just like Philip, they can't really see Collins going down. "We've all met her," Andy said of "Susan," not "Collins," adding, "She's an institution in Maine, I can't believe that Jackson can beat her." Hank was hardly alone. Everyone I spoke to at Seasons seemed to agree, even the Democrats, who have a unique affection for Collins. As the burly Hank put it, "I'll believe she loses when I see it." SUSAN COLLINS DEFIES BLUE-STATE HEADWINDS IN CRUCIAL SENATE BATTLE AS NEW POLL REVEALS STRIKING SPLIT In fairness, while Collins may be the Tom Brady of New England politics, even he lost twice to Eli Manning in the Super Bowl. So Jackson does have a chance to unseat the 73-year-old stalwart of the Senate. John and Jeff, two voters I spoke with, are hoping and voting for just that. Jeff told me his top issue this election is ICE, saying, "We shouldn't have federal troops in every city … the Portland police should be able to handle things without having immigration backing them up." FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE John went a bit further. When asked about the riots in France, he told Fox News Digital, "We should probably start rioting more in America, to be honest," but then hedged a bit with, "I would say, not riot. Protest." I met Paul at the bar of the Hollywood Casino in Bangor. He and the bartender, both in their early 70s, knew each other from the town where they grew up, "up north." Frankly, it seems like everyone in Maine knows everyone. Paul lives in South Carolina now, making him a bit of a two-for-one for this columnist. He told me he thinks the GOP will hold the Senate seat in the Palmetto State and that Maine will "come around for Susan like it always does," adding, "She has a house right up the road." The word that kept resounding in my mind as I wandered the dusty back alleys of Bangor and marveled at the sea of colors clinging to the leaves along the dusky Penobscot River was "Susan." Almost everyone I talked to called her by her first name, a level of familiarity I have rarely encountered while covering a political race. MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN The inescapable reality of this Senate campaign in Maine is that many Mainers under 40 have no memory of a time when "Susan" was not their senator. And to break that streak would require a call to arms that Troy Jackson just can't seem to muster. Among the kindest words I heard about Jackson in Bangor were those of a woman in the antiques emporium on Main Street who said, "Somebody had to run." Maine voter Wendy told Fox News Digital of Jackson, "He was a last-ditch effort," adding that she hopes Collins wins. One word I didn't hear much in Maine, and this is a problem for Jackson, is "Trump." Almost everyone I spoke with sees Collins as independent of the president, who, after all, would serve only two years of the six-year term she is running for. At Reagan National Airport on Tuesday, I bumped into former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, himself the kind of institution in my home, the Mountain State, that Collins is in Maine. He was on his way to campaign for her. The message of Manchin's mission was clear: a former Democrat, a centrist, a guy who can get things done with both sides, but also very much a former senator who could not survive the purity tests of the modern, far-left Democratic Party. For Collins' part, Republicans across the country, especially in Maine and even in the White House, are willing to look past her centrism and just be thankful a Republican has a shot in a state like Maine. articles.title: Romania blames Russia after drone sinks ship in the Black Sea
articles.summary: One sailor killed and three others missing after Comoros-flagged Khoryv hit near Romanian waters.
articles.body:
Romania has blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast, killing one crew member and leaving three others missing.

It’s the latest drone attack targeting commercial shipping off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and 30 sailors reported killed or missing in the past two weeks, raising fears of an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.

The drone struck the Comoros-flagged vessel Khoryv and its crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors on Friday, 13 nautical miles (24km) off Romania’s port of Constanta, just outside Romania’s territorial waters.

The shipping data website MarineTraffic showed the Khoryv departed Turkiye on Wednesday and was headed for Romania’s Sulina port, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea.

The canal has become the primary ‌‌‌‌route for Ukrainian exporters, which rely on ports on the Danube and Romanian territorial waters, as Russia has ‌‌‌‌attacked ‌‌‌‌Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports.

Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above ⁠⁠⁠⁠the waves as it sank.

Romania launched a rescue operation after the Khoryv sent a distress signal about 10am local time (0700 GMT).

Nine sailors were rescued, three were missing and one body was recovered during a search and rescue operation hampered by poor weather conditions and low visibility, Romania’s naval authority said.

Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to “fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities” to protect commercial shipping, after a surge in Black Sea drone attacks as fighting in Russia’s war on Ukraine escalates. NATO said on Tuesday that it would send more maritime patrol aircraft , radar systems and drones to the ⁠⁠⁠⁠Black Sea.

Romanian and European officials blamed Russia for the attack, which Romania’s President Nicusor Dan called “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”.

“It is time for Russia to take peace initiatives of the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war,” he said.

Romania’s Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Facebook that the attack was “unacceptable and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law”.

Moldova’s Foreign Ministry posted on X that “Russia’s continued escalation in the Black Sea endangers civilian lives, threatens freedom of navigation and undermines regional security”.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the attacks “reckless”, which “target innocent lives and openly defy international law.”

Russian officials did not immediately publicly comment on Friday’s sinking. It occurred after Romanian warplanes shot down two of ⁠⁠⁠⁠the latest-generation Russian drones over Romanian territorial ⁠⁠⁠⁠waters on Saturday. Russia has previously denied it is responsible for deadly drone attacks in the region.
