articles.title: Meghan did not let her father see her children to protect them
articles.summary: Today, without exactly using the word, Meghan claimed vindication.
articles.body:
Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.

Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled.

He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze.

He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren.

Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding.

Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery.

The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren.

From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close.

And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead.

Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018

Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family

Those theories became part of the case against Meghan; that she would sacrifice anyone and anything - even her father - to protect her position and save herself from any embarrassment.

That must have stung. Because today, without exactly using the word, she claimed vindication.

"I hope it can now be understood" she wrote.

"That, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."

Meghan says she was informed of the allegations back in 2018. It is understood that it was after her marriage to Harry in May that year.

Since then there has only been very limited contact between Meghan and her father - she wrote to him after he underwent surgery in the Philippines late last year.

How much all of this changes the perception of Meghan is difficult to tell. Many people have made their minds up about Meghan and the saga with her father is only part of the tangled story of the duchess and the rest of the royal family.

But her supporters will see vindication in the allegations - which have been denied by Thomas Markle - and the response that Meghan says she made when she first learned of them.

articles.title: Dónal Lunny: Celebrated Irish musician dies aged 79
articles.summary: A founding member of three renowned bands - The Bothy Band, Planxty and Moving Hearts - he was widely credited for the revival and growth of Irish traditional music.
articles.body:
One of Ireland's most-celebrated traditional musicians and multi-instrumentalists, Dónal Lunny, has died aged 79.

A founding member of three renowned bands - The Bothy Band, Planxty and Moving Hearts - he was widely credited for the revival and growth of Irish traditional music.

He also composed and wrote scores for a wide range of projects including TV dramas, documentaries and films.

In recent years he worked with contemporary artists such as Kate Bush, Rod Stewart, Elvis Costello and Clannad.

He is noted for having left a lasting impact on the music scene in Ireland and was once described by U2's Bono as the island's "answer to Quincy Jones".

Born in Tullamore, County Offaly, in 1947, Lunny moved to Newbridge in County Kildare when he was five years old and he said, from childhood, music was always an enjoyable part of his life.

He first met a young Christy Moore in 1959, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, and the two school friends recognised a musical connection between them that would last for many decades.

A founding member of Planxty with Moore, Liam O'Flynn and Andy Irvine, Lunny helped redefine traditional Irish music.

The group recorded three albums between 1971 and 1973, with Lunny playing bouzouki, guitar, keyboards and bodhrán throughout.

In 1973, he set up the label Mulligan Records and went on to produce 17 albums, with the label publishing music from a range of artists including Boomtown Rats, The Radiators and Agnes Bernell.

Lunny joined The Bothy Band in 1975, helping push the boundaries of traditional Irish music alongside Matt Molloy, Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill, Kevin Burke, Paddy Glackin and Paddy Keenan.

In 1992, Lunny produced and served as musical director of the acclaimed TV series Bringing It All Back Home, beginning a long creative partnership with producer Philip King.

He also composed film scores, including for This Is My Father, starring Aidan Quinn and James Caan.

Following a successful, decades-long career, Lunny was presented a lifetime achievement award at the BBC Radio 2 Folk Awards in 2018.

Last year, he was awarded a lifetime achievement award at the RTÉ Radio 1 Irish Folk Awards.

One of his last public appearances was in August, when he performed at the Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann [All-Ireland Fleadh] in Belfast.

Musician and composer Neil Martin, who had collaborated with Lunny throughout his career described the loss as "huge" and said he was an "extraordinary figure".

"Since the mid-60s nearly anything that was of significant movement within the traditional music world, Dónal was at the epicentral to it," he told BBC's Evening Extra programme.

Speaking of a time he shared with Dónal 18 months ago, when they sat over a drink, Neil recalled thinking "Lunny's back again" and said, although the musician had been unwell for some time, the news of his death came as "a bit of a shock".

He told the programme he was "delighted" that his last memory with Dónal is a "happy one".

"All the musicians in Ireland will have nodded to him at some stage," he added.

In a statement, The Irish Traditional Music Archive (ITMA) said Lunny's influence on Irish music was "immense" and he "opened new harmonic and rhythmic possibilities".

Crediting the work he produced in his bands, they said "his imagination shaped the sound of Irish music" and his career was described as being built on "creativity, friendship and collaboration."

"Dónal leaves behind an extraordinary body of work. His artistry, generosity and influence are woven deeply into the living tradition and into the lives of so many who knew him, were inspired by him, or had the privilege of playing and working alongside him," ITMA added.

Lunny is survived by his family including his children Oisin, Cora Venus, and Sora Chan, as well as his partner Una O'Boyle. His brother, Manus, is also a noted musician and producer.

He had a brief relationship with his musical collaborator Sinéad O'Connor in the early 2000s and they welcomed a son, Shane, in 2004.

Shane died in 2022 at the age of 17, followed by his mother in 2023.

articles.title: Many feared trapped after multistorey building collapses in Kenya
articles.summary: Officials say building in Nairobi’s Eastleigh area had no occupation certificate, but ground floor was in use.
articles.body:
Many people are feared to be trapped in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, after a multistorey building under construction collapsed, leaving a huge mound of concrete as rescuers dig through the rubble.

The building came down on Friday at about 1pm local time (10:00GMT) on a busy commercial street in Eastleigh, a neighbourhood crowded with thousands of traders and residents.

Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said more than 10 upper floors were under construction. The ground floor had been rented to an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi, reporting from Nairobi, said the developers and authorities are being asked “to answer now” as people were not supposed to be inside a building under construction.

She said rescue efforts were expected to continue through Friday night and Saturday.

Rescuers used poles stripped from trees and excavators to move concrete bound with steel, as heavy equipment was slow to arrive.

Mohamud said one injured woman had been rescued and taken to hospital, while another person who had been calling for help had gone silent. He warned of a potential second collapse because the building was leaning on its neighbour.

Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse and police firing tear gas to disperse crowds.

Joseph Kaula, a plasterer working on the fifth floor of the collapsed building, told AP that he was the last person to walk out.

“The whole area was filled with dust,” he said.

Relatives of those trapped said some had phoned for help immediately after the collapse, but their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up to report missing relatives.

“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters.

He said the building had been approved for construction but had no certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was illegal.

“This has potentially cost lives,” he told reporters on site.

He said that it was possible “one or two” people had died and that more would be known as time went on.

Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked approvals, according to the AFP news agency.

Sakaja said county governments needed stronger enforcement powers, calling lenient penalties a “slap on the wrist”. Police said they would carry out investigations and anyone found negligent would face the law.

articles.title: 2 bank branch managers under scanner in Rs 7.3-crore mule-account racket
articles.summary: Delhi Police probe a Rs 7.3-crore mule-account cybercrime racket; two private bank branch managers under scanner, six arrested, 37 accounts tied to 99 cases.
articles.body: New Delhi: Two branch managers of a private bank are under the scanner for allegedly facilitating a mule-account racket that channelled cybercrime proceeds worth Rs 7.3 crore.Six people, including Shobhit Aggarwal, branch manager of the bank’s Saraswati Vihar branch, have been arrested, while Sushant Kumar, branch manager of the Tri Nagar branch, is absconding. Police are also probing alleged cryptocurrency transactions linked to the network and a suspected connection to a Chinese national.The racket surfaced during scrutiny of suspicious accounts at the Tri Nagar branch. Police found that some account holders had allegedly never visited the branch, while addresses linked to several accounts could not be verified. Many of the accounts were linked to cybercrime complaints registered across the country.As the probe expanded, investigators identified 17 more suspicious accounts. Police alleged that photographs and KYC documents had not been captured through the prescribed live-verification process and that several addresses were non-existent.A technical analysis of mobile numbers, email IDs and linked devices led police to Mayank Kapoor, alleged to be the operator of the mule-account network. He was arrested from Baba Haridas Nagar.During interrogation, Kapoor allegedly disclosed that he collected identity documents and photographs from daily-wage labourers on the pretext of arranging loans and then used them to open bank accounts.Police alleged that Aggarwal facilitated the opening of accounts without the physical presence of account holders and using forged signatures. He allegedly introduced Kapoor to Kumar, expanding the operation across both branches. Sales staff Manoj, Ankur, Fatma and Pankaj allegedly processed the accounts, which were approved by the branch managers.Investigators have identified around 37 suspected mule accounts linked to 99 cybercrime complaints nationwide, with nearly Rs 7.3 crore credited into them. Police alleged that part of the proceeds was shared with bank officials, while the remaining amount was converted into USDT cryptocurrency through Trust Wallet.Aggarwal and the four sales staff members were arrested after investigators gathered what they described as sufficient evidence. articles.title: Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska
articles.summary: The lawsuit raises concerns the US administration may be looking to meddle in some of this midterm cycle’s races.
articles.body:
With just more than a week until the pivotal US midterm elections, the US Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the results in Alaska’s hotly contested Senate race.

In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the Justice Department argued that an independent candidate with the same name as the state’s incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan , who is currently running for re-election, is purposefully running to mislead voters.

“Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Daniel J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan, and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity,” the Trump administration’s filing read.

The Justice Department is asking a federal judge to delay certification to allow time for an investigation into “whether votes cast for Daniel J Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”.

The lawsuit raises concerns by Democrats and voting rights groups that the Trump administration may be looking to meddle in some of the upcoming midterm races as Republicans across the United States struggle to push back a growing wave of Democratic support.

The Justice Department, as of late, has taken several actions against Democratic critics of President Donald Trump that have bolstered those worries, including charging a high-ranking Virginia lawmaker, state Senator L Louise Lucas, in a public corruption case and launching a probe into Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar over allegations of immigration fraud. Both have said the actions are politically motivated.

Trump critics have long expressed worries that the Justice Department could seek to block certification of elections the US president’s party loses.

On Wednesday, as Lucas’s indictment was announced, US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters his agency would not do so unless extreme circumstances warranted such action.

“It is not DOJ’s intention to – and it’s never our intention to – improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” Blanche said.

The Brennan Center for Justice’s senior counsel, Lauren Miller Karalunas, said in a statement that election certification is handled by US states and the federal government has “no role” in it.

“Rest assured, state certification processes were created to meet this moment,” Karalunas said. “Centuries ago, state legislatures recognized that bad actors could use the process to manipulate election outcomes. They built in safeguards specifically designed to stop that from happening.”

The Alaska state Supreme Court in June rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J Sullivan from the ballot. He will appear without a party designation by his name, while Senator Sullivan will be listed as the Republican candidate.

However, under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, voters can select both Sullivans if they are unsure.

Which party controls the US Senate after November 3 could, ultimately, come down to Alaska’s Senate race, where Senator Sullivan is engaged in a challenging re-election fight against former US Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola.

Polling of the race has consistently shown a race that is well within the margin of error. A survey conducted by Public Policy Polling earlier this month suggested Peltola had a narrow one-point lead.

The campaign teams for both Sullivans and Peltola did not immediately return requests for comment.

articles.summary: ESPN host Michael Wilbon unleashed an expletive-filled rant on "The Dan LeBatard Show," accusing The New York Times of gutting its sports news coverage.
articles.body: Longtime ESPN host Michael Wilbon unleashed an expletive-laced rant against The New York Times on Wednesday, blasting the paper over its treatment of sports writers. While appearing on "The Dan Le Batard Show," host Dan Le Batard pointed out that The New York Times was the only major publication that did not allow its sports writers to appear on Wilbon's ESPN show "Pardon the Interruption." Wilbon, who began his career in print journalism and spent decades at The Washington Post before joining ESPN full-time in 2010, accused the Times of abandoning the sports writing industry. FRANK ISOLA COMMENTS ON MICHAEL WILBON NAMING HIM PREFERRED 'PTI' CO-HOST WHEN TONY KORNHEISER RETIRES "They bailed," Wilbon said. "They were the first to bail. F--- The New York Times. I work for a better section anyway. You think I wouldn’t take a section with Tom Boswell and Dave Kindred and Tony Kornheiser and Sally Jenkins and David Remnick and David Aldridge and J.A. Adande — and I’m skipping a whole generation of people — Barry Lorge, the greatest tennis writer of all time? Half those people went to television. "F--- The New York Times, which bailed on our profession. It bailed. It took the sports section away. Gutless motherf------!" Fox News Digital reached out to The New York Times for comment. ESPN declined to comment. THE ATHLETIC EXECUTIVE EDITOR ADMITS KEY MISTAKE MADE IN HANDLING OF DIANNA RUSSINI CONTROVERSY: REPORT Wilbon was likely referring to The New York Times announcing in 2023 that it would be closing its internal sports department and instead focus on covering teams and games through The Athletic, which it acquired one year earlier. Though there were no layoffs from the acquisition, the sports department at the Times had grown smaller and smaller in the years prior to the purchase. The desk eventually lost its stand-alone section in the daily print edition, and local teams were no longer guaranteed an assigned beat reporter. New York Times staffers have since petitioned to have The Athletic staffers join their union. articles.title: Meghalaya tourism dept allays concerns over Shillong Peak Ropeway
articles.summary: Meghalaya tourism dept says Shillong Peak Ropeway won’t impact sacred Lum Shillong catchment; Rs151cr PM-DevINE/NDB project to cut traffic, pollution.
articles.body: Shillong: Meghalaya’s tourism department held a stakeholders’ meeting to clarify concerns over the proposed Shillong Peak Ropeway Project’s impact on the Lum Shillong catchment.The meeting, chaired by tourism commissioner and secretary R M Kurbah, was attended by officials from various departments, members of the Riat Laban Dorbar Pyllun and representatives of the Joint Action Committee. The meeting was held on Thursday.Meghalaya Ropeway Development Authority (MRDA) CEO CVD Diengdoh said the Rs 151-crore project would be funded by the New Development Bank and the Centre under the PM-DevINE scheme.The proposed 913-metre ropeway would use a monocable gondola system and connect Madan Laban to an upper terminal near the existing Shillong Viewpoint. The journey is expected to take five to six minutes.Diengdoh said the project was conceived to improve access to the viewpoint, one of Meghalaya’s most visited tourist destinations. Access is currently regulated because the route passes through defence land.He said the project would create direct and indirect employment and support vendors’ livelihoods.Diengdoh said the electrically powered ropeway would produce no operational smoke.
